Just how much money was received from land sales and how many of the proposed projects were accomplished was apparently never clearly understood by the Crow people. It was obvious, however, that the anticipated land boom did not materialize. The Government later decided to give some of the vacant and unclaimed land in the Ceded Area back to the original owners. Thus in 1926 and again in 1928, the Government allotted 160 acre tracts to many Crow children. Since that time these Ceded Strip allotments have been leased or sold to local non-Indian ranchers.
The influx of whites to the area continued at a substantial rate until around 1940. During this period Big Horn County was established (1913) and its county seat, Hardin, was settled (1907). In the 1930's the reservation's agricultural environment was significantly disrupted by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), which gave the Crows job opportunities but forced them to leave their land and homes. Because these jobs required that people travel, many of the Crows sold their equipment and leased or sold their land.
By the 1950's much of the Indian population on the reservation was clustered around the communities of Crow Agency, Lodge Grass, Wyola, and in the Little Big Horn Valley. Social disorganization and poverty had become acute. The issuance of grazing permits and the selling of individually-owned lands placed control of much of the Indian reservation lands in non-Indian hands (Crow Reservation Comprehensive Plan: The Population and Economy, 1971, p. 275).
